title: Mini project 2: revision quiz
specPoints: 2.1.1–2.1.2 Decomposition, designing algorithms in pseudocode; 2.2.3 random numbers, string manipulation, lists, file handling, sub programs
2.3.1–2.3.2 Validation, maintainability, test plans and refining; 2.1.3 searching and sorting a list
Practical programming skills (Section B): build a complete program from a brief with less scaffolding
learn: Decompose a nine-requirement brief into pure functions (testable with assert) and screens (tested through the menu)
Design and implement random selection without repeats
Compare answers ignoring case and spaces; filter a list by a field; find the top n of a list
Use a file in append mode for a log and compare it with the whole-file rewrite used before
Write the test plan and evaluation with less guidance than project 1
hook: Project 1 gave you the file handling, the helpers and the main loop. This time you get the brief, the data files and a skeleton of function names with docstrings — nothing else. The docstrings are the design. Half the functions are 'pure': they take values and return values, so you can prove them right with assert before you build a single menu.

video.title: Pure functions first
video.brief: 4 minutes. The quiz brief, numbered. The skeleton with its two groups: pure functions (categories, filter, pick, check, top) and screens (choose category, play, high scores, menu). Asserts run against the pure functions — one fails: `pick_questions` returned a repeat; the fix uses a copy and `pop`. Then the screens are built on top and a quiz is played: three Maths questions, two right, 67%, score saved. High scores show the top five. End with the test plan's boundary rows highlighted.

explain.code:
BRIEF: A revision quiz that reads its questions from a file.

R1  Load questions from questions.txt (category,question,answer per line).        [1]
R2  Validated menu: Play, High scores, Categories, Quit; repeat until Quit.         [1]
R3  Before playing, show the categories numbered plus an 'All' option and let      [2]
    the user choose one.
R4  Ask the user how many questions (1 to the number available); choose them at    [2]
    random with no repeats.
R5  Accept answers in any case and ignore spaces around them.                        [1]
R6  Keep the score; after a wrong answer show the correct one; at the end show      [2]
    score, total and percentage (whole number).
R7  Ask for the player's name and append name,score,total to highscores.txt.        [1]
R8  High scores option shows the best 5 by score, highest first.                    [2]
R9  All input validated; if fewer questions exist than asked for, use all of them;  [1]
    the program must not crash on a missing or faulty file.
                                                                           Total [13]

p: Split the functions into two groups. **Pure functions** take values and return values and never use `input` or `print`: `categories`, `filter_by_category`, `pick_questions`, `check_answer`, `top_scores`. Test them with `assert` before anything else. **Screens** talk to the user: `choose_category`, `play_quiz`, `show_high_scores`, `show_menu`. They are short because they call the pure functions. This split is what makes a program testable, and it is what the examiner means by 'use subprograms appropriately'.
explain.code:
Pure (assert-tested)                    Screen (menu-tested)
check_answer(" PARIS ", "Paris") → True   play_quiz: ask, call check_answer, score
pick_questions(qs, 3) → 3 different      choose_category: print list, get_int
filter_by_category(qs, "Maths") → 4 qs   show_high_scores: load_scores, top_scores, print
top_scores(scores, 5) → best 5

explain.h: Two designs worth writing in pseudocode first
p: **Random without repeats**: copy the list, then `how_many` times pick a random index, `pop` it from the copy and append it to the result. The copy matters — popping from the real list would delete questions. **Top n**: sort a copy by score descending (`sorted(scores, key=..., reverse=True)` or a bubble sort), then take the first `min(n, len)` items. Both have a boundary at 'fewer items than asked for' — that is R9, and it is a test row.
explain.code:
function pickQuestions(questions, howMany)
    pool = copy of questions
    chosen = empty list
    if howMany > pool.length then howMany = pool.length endif
    for i = 1 to howMany
        index = random(0, pool.length - 1)
        chosen.append(pool[index])
        pool.remove(index)
    next i
    return chosen
endfunction

p: Project 1 rewrote the whole book file with `"w"` because records changed. High scores are a **log**: nothing is ever edited, lines are only added, so `"a"` (append) is right and simpler — one line per game. Reading them back is the same `split(",")` and cast pattern. Note the design consequence: the top-5 is computed when displayed, not stored.
A quiz. Questions come from a file. Pick a category and how many. Random questions, no repeats. Score at the end. Save the score. Show the best five.

list: **Pure**: value in, value out. No input or print. Test with `assert`.
**Screens**: talk to the user. Call the pure functions.

p: Copy the list. Pick a random position. Take that question out of the copy and add it to the chosen list. Repeat.

keyterms.def: A function whose result depends only on its parameters and that has no input, output or other side effects.
Anything a function does besides returning a value, such as printing, reading input or changing a file.
Choosing items at random so that no item can be chosen twice.
Opening a file with `"a"` so new lines are added at the end and existing lines are kept.
Producing a new list containing only the items that meet a condition.
A file that only ever has lines added, such as a record of every game played.

try.title: 1. Decompose and design (paper, 10 minutes)
p: Number the requirements. List nouns → data (what is a question record? what is a score record? which file is rewritten and which is appended?). List verbs → functions, and sort them into pure and screen. Draw the structure diagram. Then write **OCR pseudocode** for `check_answer` and for `top_scores` (a bubble sort or a repeated 'find the max and remove' are both fine). Keep the paper: you will compare it with your code.

try.title: 2. Build it from the skeleton
p: Only stubs and docstrings. Build in this order and **run after each**: (1) paste your helpers from lesson 3; (2) `load_questions` — print how many loaded; (3) the five pure functions — write at least two `assert` lines for each at the bottom before moving on; (4) `choose_category` and `show_menu`; (5) `play_quiz` with `save_score`; (6) `show_high_scores`. The data files are provided; `highscores.txt` already has three lines.

try.title: 3. Prove the pure functions
p: Paste your five pure functions over the stubs here and run. Every assert must pass. Then add asserts of your own for: `check_answer("8", "8 ")`, `pick_questions` on an empty list, `top_scores` with fewer than 5 records, `categories` when a category appears twice, `filter_by_category(qs, "All")`. One of the given asserts is deliberately strict about repeats — if it fails, read the pseudocode in the lesson again.

try.title: 4. Test plan, run, evaluate
p: Write the plan (at least 16 rows) before the final run. Rows you must include: number of questions = 1 and = all available (boundary); number = available + 1 (invalid); answer in capitals with spaces (normal for R5); a category with exactly one question; empty `highscores.txt` (delete its contents); `questions.txt` with a bad line. Run, log, fix, re-run. Then the evaluation table R1–R9 with test evidence, and three sentences on robustness, maintainability and one limitation.
steps: Percentage: 2 out of 3 should show 67, not 66.66666 — which rounding did you use, and is 0 out of 0 possible?
Which functions did your assert harness prove, and which could only be tested through the menu? Say so in the evaluation.

opts: Returns a value that depends only on its parameters
check.fb: No input, no print, no side effects — easy to assert.

check.q: To pick questions at random with no repeats you should:
opts: Copy the list and pop each chosen item from the copy
check.fb: Removing from a copy prevents repeats and protects the original.

check.q: `check_answer(" paris", "Paris")` should return True. The implementation needs:
check.fb: Strip spaces and match case on both sides.

check.q: The high-score file is opened with `"a"` rather than `"w"` because:
opts: Scores are only ever added, never changed, so append keeps the old ones

exam.q: Write a function `percentage(score, total)` that returns the score as a whole-number percentage of the total, returning 0 if the total is 0.
model: Function header with both parameters (1). Check for total equal to 0 returning 0 (1). Otherwise return `round(score / total * 100)` or integer division equivalent (1).
exam.commentary: The zero check is a mark — dividing by zero is the crash the brief warns about. `int()` truncates (66) while `round()` gives 67; either accepted if consistent, but state which.

exam.q: A quiz program chooses questions with `random.randint(0, len(questions) - 1)` inside a loop and asks `questions[index]` each time. A tester reports that the same question was asked twice in one game. Explain why and describe how the program should be refined.
model: Each random index is independent so the same index can be generated more than once (1). Keep a list of indexes already used and re-pick when a repeat occurs, or remove each chosen question from a copy of the list (1). Also ensure the number requested cannot exceed the number available, to avoid an endless re-pick (1).
exam.commentary: Cause, refinement, and the edge case the refinement creates. The third mark separates students who have built it from those who have read about it.

exam.q: The high-score file stores `name,score,total`. Describe how the program finds the five highest scores to display.
model: Read every line, split at the commas and store the records in a list with the score cast to an integer (1). Sort the list by score in descending order, e.g. with a bubble sort or a sort function (1). Output the first five records, or all of them if there are fewer than five (1).
exam.commentary: Describe = what/how in order. Casting is needed because `"9" > "10"` as strings. The fewer-than-five case is the boundary mark.

home: Refine the quiz so a question answered wrongly is asked again at the end of the game (once), and the final score counts only first attempts. Write the three test rows that prove it and update the evaluation.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 2 · explain 8 · Try 1 paper 10 · Try 2–3 build 30 · Try 4 plan and evaluation 8 · homework 2. Realistically a lesson and a half; if so, end lesson 1 after the pure functions pass (Try 3) and start lesson 2 with the screens.
misconceptions: Popping chosen questions from the real list, so the quiz destroys its own question bank.
Comparing scores read from the file as strings, so '9' beats '10'.
`check_answer` that strips one side only, or lowercases the given answer but not the correct one.
Asking for the number of questions before the category is known, so the range is wrong.
